title: How Tech Works · Episode 4
chapters: How GPS knows where you are

units.t: How Tech Works. Episode four.
In this episode: How GPS knows where you are, How encryption keeps secrets and Blockchain, simply.
Part one. How GPS knows where you are.
Your phone finds you to within a few metres by listening to ultra-precise clocks orbiting high above the Earth.
Listening to satellites.
The Global Positioning System is run by the US and uses a constellation of around 31 satellites orbiting about 20,200 kilometres above Earth.
Each one constantly broadcasts, in effect, "I'm this satellite, here's my position, and this is the exact time."
Your phone doesn't send anything back.
It only listens.
By measuring how long each signal took to arrive, it works out how far away each satellite is.
That distance is the starting point for everything else GPS does.
Pinning down your position.
If you're exactly 20,500 km from one satellite, you could be anywhere on a giant sphere around it.
A second satellite narrows that to a circle.
A third narrows it to two points, one of which is usually far out in space.
This process is called trilateration.
A fourth satellite is needed because your phone's clock isn't perfectly accurate.
Your device usually uses many more satellites for better accuracy.
Timing matters enormously.
Signals travel at the speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres per second, so an error of one millionth of a second would put you out by about 300 metres.
That's why each satellite carries atomic clocks accurate to billionths of a second.
Blurred on purpose.
GPS began as a US military project.
The first satellite launched in 1978, and the full system was declared operational in 1995.
For years the military deliberately added errors to the civilian signal, a feature called Selective Availability.
Ordinary receivers were accurate to only about 100 metres, while military users got precise positions.
In May 2000, on the orders of President Bill Clinton, it was switched off.
Civilian accuracy improved roughly tenfold overnight, helping spark the boom in car navigation, fitness trackers and smartphone maps.
The US later announced that newer satellites would be built without the ability to degrade the signal at all.
Many systems, fast fixes.
GPS isn't the only system.
Russia runs GLONASS, the European Union runs Galileo, and China runs BeiDou.
Together they're called GNSS, global navigation satellite systems.
Most phones use several at once, seeing more satellites and getting faster, more accurate fixes.
Australia is building SouthPAN, which improves accuracy across Australia and New Zealand for farming, mining, aviation and emergency services.
A standalone receiver can be slow to lock on, because it downloads satellite data slowly from space.
Your phone downloads it over the internet and also estimates your location from mobile towers and Wi-Fi networks.
That's why it can find you almost instantly, even indoors.
Limits and uses.
GPS signals are weak by the time they reach Earth and can't pass through buildings or ground.
In city centres they bounce off tall buildings, making your blue dot jump around; this is the urban canyon effect.
Tunnels and dense forest can block them entirely.
Phones are typically accurate to about five metres under open sky, while surveying and farming equipment can reach centimetre accuracy.
GPS guides planes and ships, helps emergency services find people and lets tractors drive straight lines to save fuel and fertiliser.
Its timing keeps mobile networks, power grids and stock exchanges in sync.
The US opened GPS to civilian use after a Korean Air Lines plane strayed into Soviet airspace and was shot down in 1983.
The key idea: GPS works by timing signals from satellites, with your phone listening only and never transmitting.
Part two. How encryption keeps secrets.
The maths behind the padlock in your browser, and why it protects nearly everything you do online.
Scrambling secrets.
Encryption turns readable information, called plaintext, into scrambled data, called ciphertext, using a key.
Only someone with the right key can turn it back.
It quietly protects your messages, passwords, banking, medical records and card payments.
Without it, anyone who could intercept internet traffic, such as someone on the same public Wi-Fi, could read what you send.
Secret codes are ancient.
Julius Caesar is said to have shifted each letter three places along the alphabet, so A became D.
Such ciphers fall to frequency analysis: E is the most common letter in English, so the most common symbol probably stands for E.
The Arab scholar al-Kindi described this in the 9th century.
Enigma and the codebreakers.
In World War II, Germany used the Enigma machine.
Its rotating wheels scrambled each letter differently, creating an astronomical number of possible settings, and the settings changed daily.
Building on earlier work by Polish mathematicians, British codebreakers at Bletchley Park, including Alan Turing, built machines to find those daily settings.
The intelligence helped the Allies win the Battle of the Atlantic and is thought to have shortened the war.
The effort also helped lay the foundations for modern computing.
One key or two.
In symmetric encryption, the same key locks and unlocks the data.
Ciphers like the widely used AES standard are fast and extremely secure, so they protect files, phones and most internet traffic.
The problem is sharing the key.
For centuries, keys had to be delivered physically, by couriers or in person.
In 1976, Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published a revolutionary idea, and in 1977 Rivest, Shamir and Adleman created RSA.
Public-key encryption uses two linked keys.
Your public key can be shared with anyone to lock messages to you.
Only your private key unlocks them.
Think of a padlock anyone can snap shut, but only you can open.
The padlock in your browser.
When you see HTTPS and a padlock, a protocol called TLS is protecting the connection.
Your browser checks the site's digital certificate, issued by a trusted authority, to confirm it's the real site.
The two then use public-key techniques to agree on a shared secret key, and switch to fast symmetric encryption for the rest of the session.
The padlock means the connection is encrypted, not that the website is trustworthy.
Scam sites can have padlocks too.
Why it's hard to break.
Modern encryption relies on maths that is easy to do one way and extremely hard to reverse.
Multiplying two huge prime numbers is easy for a computer.
Working out which two primes made the result is enormously hard.
Guessing a 256-bit key by brute force would take longer than the age of the universe.
So attackers rarely break the maths.
They steal passwords, trick people or exploit software bugs.
Apps like Signal, WhatsApp and iMessage use end-to-end encryption, so only sender and recipient can read messages.
Future quantum computers could break some public-key systems, so new post-quantum standards were published in 2024.
The key idea: Encryption uses a key to turn readable plaintext into scrambled ciphertext that only the key holder can reverse.
Part three. Blockchain, simply.
What a blockchain actually is, what it's good for, and what it isn't, without the crypto hype.
Trust without a middleman.
Normally, when you send money online, a trusted middleman such as your bank keeps the official record of who owns what.
Digital files are easy to copy, so without that middleman, how would anyone stop you spending the same digital dollar twice?
A blockchain is a way for many people who don't know or trust each other to agree on a shared record, with no central authority.
It's a list of records, usually transactions, that thousands of computers keep identical copies of, often called a distributed ledger.
Anyone can check it, and no single person or company controls it.
Blocks in a chain.
Transactions are grouped into blocks.
Each block includes a hash of the block before it.
A hash is a digital fingerprint: a short code calculated from the data, which changes completely if even one character changes.
Because each block holds the previous block's fingerprint, the blocks link into a chain.
Change anything in an old block and its fingerprint changes, breaking every link after it.
Because so many copies exist, you can't quietly rewrite history in one place, and everyone else would immediately notice.
Agreeing without a boss.
The network needs a way to decide who adds the next block.
Bitcoin uses proof of work: computers called miners compete to solve a hard mathematical puzzle, and the winner adds the block and earns new bitcoin.
It's deliberately expensive, which makes cheating costly.
Ethereum switched in 2022 to proof of stake.
Participants lock up their own coins as a guarantee of good behaviour and risk losing them if they cheat.
That cut Ethereum's energy use by more than 99%.
Bitcoin, launched in 2009 by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto, was the first blockchain, with supply capped at 21 million coins.
Ethereum, launched in 2015, added smart contracts: programs on the blockchain that carry out an agreement automatically when set conditions are met.
Useful, but costly.

Blockchains are genuinely useful when many parties need a shared, tamper-resistant record and don't want to trust one middleman: sending money across borders, tracking supply chains or proving ownership of a digital item.
But many proposed uses would work as well, or better, with an ordinary database run by a trusted organisation.
A good question is: why does this need a blockchain?
Removing the middleman has costs.
Public blockchains can be slower and more expensive than card networks.
Bitcoin's electricity use has been estimated to be comparable to that of a mid-sized country.
Transactions generally can't be reversed, and if you lose your wallet's private key, there's no customer service.
Your coins are gone.
Crypto and risk.
Thousands of other cryptocurrencies exist.
Many have collapsed, and some were outright scams.

Prices are extremely volatile; a coin can lose most of its value within weeks, and money held on a crypto exchange isn't protected by the government's Financial Claims Scheme the way bank deposits are.
In 2025, AUSTRAC, Australia's financial crime regulator, limited cash transactions at crypto ATMs to $5,000 after finding they were heavily used by scam victims, many of them older Australians.
Crypto is also a favoured scam payment because transfers are fast and hard to reverse.
If you choose to invest, use only money you can afford to lose, use reputable Australian-registered exchanges, and be deeply sceptical of anyone promising guaranteed returns.
This is general information only.
The key idea: A blockchain lets strangers agree on a shared record without a central authority in charge.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. How does your phone work out its distance from a GPS satellite?
Answer. By timing how long its signal takes to arrive.
Question two. Why can't someone on the same public Wi-Fi read your encrypted messages?
Answer. They lack the key to unscramble the data.
Question three. What problem does a blockchain solve?
Answer. Letting strangers agree on a shared record.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
